extracted.intended_audience: mathematics students, researchers, and contributors to a 'Tricks Wiki' interested in proof techniques and existence/construction problems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for proving existence statements by building the desired object one element at a time (possibly transfinitely), with emphasis on reformulation to countable constraints, ordering of tasks, and methods to ensure continuation at each step. Includes examples, anti-examples, and technical caveats (cardinality arguments, transfinite induction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'just-do-it' proof
rubrics_metrics.description: "A just-do-it proof is one that builds a sequence (x_n) that satisfies a sequence of constraints P_n, where the n-th constraint, P_n, is a property of x_n, and where for any sequence (x_1,...,x_{n-1}) that satisfies P_1,...,P_{n-1} it is not hard to prove that there exists x_n such that the sequence (x_1,...,x_n) satisfies P_1,...,P_n."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core criterion: set up the problem as constructing a sequence (or well-ordered chain) of objects with local constraints so that at each step one can choose a next element without difficulty. The entry includes multiple worked examples (dense set in plane, 2-colouring integers, sets with large symmetric difference, Cantor-type construction, infinite matrix, transfinite construction) illustrating the definition. Anti-pattern: trying to 'define the whole set at once' rather than inductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulate uncountable/continuous constraints into countable ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace uncountably many conditions (e.g. for every real point and every positive real epsilon) by an equivalent countable set of conditions (e.g. rationals and epsilons of the form 1/m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to construct a dense subset of the plane avoid dealing with all points and epsilons by taking rational-coordinate points and epsilons 1/m, turning the problem into satisfying a countable family of open discs. This reduction is often a preliminary and crucial simplification before applying a just-do-it construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure each step has only finitely (or < problematic cardinality) many forbidden choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When adding the n-th element one should only have to avoid finitely many 'bad' points/lines/circles so that the ambient set (open disc, circle, continuum) still contains allowable choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in the plane-dense construction one must avoid only finitely many lines and finitely many previously chosen points when selecting the next point in a disc; in the symmetric-difference construction there are only at most 2^{o(N)} forbidden sets. Use elementary arguments (an open disc cannot be covered by finitely many lines and points; a circle has continuum many points while the set to avoid has smaller cardinality) to justify existence of a choice. Anti-pattern: if the set of forbidden positions is large (e.g. dense or of full measure) the method fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count/measure/cardinality arguments to guarantee available choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use simple counting, binomial-coefficient bounds, or cardinality comparisons (continuum vs fewer) to show the number of forbidden options is strictly less than the number of possible options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for symmetric-difference codes, count the number of sets at small symmetric difference (≤k) from a given set and show it's ≤ c^N with c<2, so if you need exponentially many sets you can continue. Example (transfinite): each circle has continuum many points while the number of points to avoid is of smaller cardinality, so one can pick a new point. These quantitative arguments are part of the 'it is not hard to continue' justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate ordering/enumeration of tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an ordering (enumeration) of the constraints/tasks that makes the inductive construction possible — sometimes alternating types rather than doing all of one type first is crucial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for the infinite matrix with row-limits and column-limits, enumerate as row1, col1, row2, col2, ... so each step imposes only finitely many compatibility constraints. Anti-pattern: doing all rows first then all columns can make constraints unmanageable. This criterion includes being explicit about the indexing/order of tasks to avoid global conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfinite induction / well-ordering when index-set is uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: If constraints are indexed by an uncountable set (e.g. positive reals), use a well-ordering of that set and perform induction along the well-ordering (defining objects for each ordinal), handling successor and limit stages appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 6: well-order the positive reals, index them by ordinals, and at each ordinal either take union of earlier stages or add a point chosen to realize the required distance while avoiding fewer-than-continuum forbidden points. Caveats: this uses the well-ordering theorem (equivalent to axiom of choice) and requires checking predecessor-cardinality bounds so that the avoidance arguments still work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit-stage handling in transfinite constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: At a limit ordinal λ, define the object at stage λ as the union (or natural limit) of the earlier objects; ensure the induction hypothesis includes properties preserved under unions/limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the transfinite distance example, the construction keeps sets A_α increasing; at limit stages A_λ = ⋃_{β<λ} A_β. Ensure hypotheses (no duplicated distances, every earlier index's distance realized) are preserved under unions. Also ensure a rule that at most one point is added per step (or otherwise control cardinalities) to keep avoidance arguments valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reformulate the target property to local/pointwise constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite global existence demands as a collection of local constraints about membership or values that can be attended to sequentially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: colouring integers so that every infinite arithmetic progression contains both colours becomes: enumerate progressions and for each choose one red and one blue element not used before; Cantor's diagonal/interval method: require at step n that the chosen interval avoid the nth listed algebraic number. This reformulation is a standard pre-step to the just-do-it approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of where just-do-it is unlikely to work (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technique is ineffective when constraints are too global, algebraic, or tightly coupled so that local choices soon eliminate future options (e.g., constructing Hadamard matrices of given order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terry Tao's remark (quoted) and Gowers' commentary describe that just-do-it fails when constraints are global or algebraic, or when the problem sits 'in between' too-few and too-many constraints. In such cases one may need stronger ideas or to prove a stronger result to reduce the search space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive vs explicit: just-do-it often gives a method but not a closed formula
rubrics_metrics.description: A just-do-it proof typically provides an explicit algorithm/procedure to generate the object but may not yield a simple closed-form description of the final object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cantor-style construction yields a constructive algorithm (nested intervals) but not an explicit transcendental number formula. Note: with extra care one can sometimes make the procedure fully algorithmic by approximating roots etc., but explicit formulae may remain elusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care to avoid duplicating previously achieved properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating a new element to realize a new constraint, ensure it does not accidentally violate prior constraints or create undesired duplicates (e.g. duplicate a previously used distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Example 6: when adding a point to realize a new distance r from some existing point, also avoid points that would create the same r with other pairs or would duplicate existing distances; this may require avoiding intersections of bisecting lines and circles. Keep the induction hypothesis precise so these checks are accounted for. Gowers' comments add that one should also ensure at most one point is added per stage to control cardinality of avoided points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple geometric/topological facts as existence arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on elementary facts like: an open disc cannot be covered by finitely many points and lines; a circle has continuum cardinality; one can always find a subinterval of half length avoiding a specified real number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These small lemmas are used repeatedly to justify 'there is no difficulty in choosing' the next element. The blog supplies short proofs or sketches for such facts when needed (e.g., pick a line through center not parallel to finitely many given lines, then avoid finitely many intersection points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative enumeration/counting bounds in combinatorial settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply explicit counting arguments (e.g., bounding number of small symmetric-difference sets by binomial coefficients) to show enough unused choices remain at each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 3: to choose exponentially many subsets pairwise with symmetric difference ≥k, bound number of sets within distance ≤k of a given set by ≤(sum binomials) ≤ c^N with c<2, which ensures the greedy inductive selection can continue while 2^N grows faster. This is the standard combinatorial variant of the 'avoid only few bad choices' principle.
